lesson.intro: Two pointers turns many O(n^2) pair-checking solutions into O(n) scans. Learn its three shapes, the elimination argument that proves each move is safe, and the duplicate handling that trips people up in 3sum.
objectives: Recognize two-pointer problems and pick the right shape
Justify each pointer move with an elimination argument
Implement pair sum, palindromes, in-place dedupe and 3sum
State the cost of two-pointer and sort-then-sweep solutions

sections.title: Recognizing a two-pointer problem
sections.key: Two pointers keep two indexes and move them so every step rules something out for good, turning O(n^2) pair checks into O(n) scans.
sections.body:
You have sorted gift prices and want two that use a gift card exactly. Trying every pair is O(n^2). But the list is sorted, so moving an index changes a sum in a predictable direction.

**Two pointers** keeps two indexes into a sequence, or one per sequence, and moves them based on what it sees. It comes in three shapes:

[[visual]]

Signals in a problem statement:

- The input is sorted, or sorting loses nothing you need.
- You need a pair or triple with a target sum or difference.
- "In place" or "O(1) extra space" for an array or string.
- You compare from both ends, as in palindromes.

It does not fit when you need original positions in unsorted data (two sum on unsorted input uses a hash map), or when moving a pointer has no predictable effect.

visual.title: Three shapes
rows: Start at both ends and move inward
Pair sums in sorted arrays, palindromes, reversing, container with most water
Both move left to right at different speeds
Read and write pointers for in-place filtering; fast and slow pointers on linked lists
Merging two sorted arrays, subsequence checks

sections.tip: If a problem gives you a sorted array and you are about to write a nested loop over pairs, stop and try converging pointers first.

check.question: Which problem is the weakest fit for converging two pointers?
choices: Two sum on a sorted array
Checking whether a string is a palindrome
Two sum on an unsorted array where you must return the original indexes
Reversing an array in place
check.explanation: Converging pointers rely on sorted order. Sorting an unsorted array would scramble the indexes you must return, so a one-pass hash map is the better tool there. The other three are classic converging-pointer problems.

sections.title: Opposite ends: pair sum in a sorted array
sections.key: On sorted data, move `lo` right when the sum is too small and `hi` left when it is too big: each move discards a value that fits no remaining pair.
sections.body:
Sorted `[1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11]`, target 10. Start with `lo` at the smallest value and `hi` at the largest.

[[visual]]

Why is each move safe? When the sum is too big, every remaining partner for `nums[hi]` is at least `nums[lo]`, so every pair using `nums[hi]` is too big too. Discard it. Too small is the mirror image.

Each step eliminates one value, so the pointers meet within n - 1 steps: O(n) time, O(1) space. Loop `while lo < hi`, because a value cannot pair with itself.

**Counting pairs below a target:** when `nums[lo] + nums[hi]` is small enough, `nums[lo]` works with every index up to hi, so add `hi - lo` at once and move lo.

visual.title: Target 10
visual.caption: Gray values are eliminated for good.

sections.tip: Interviewers often ask why the move is safe. Say: "each move discards a value that cannot be in any remaining pair."
sections.pitfall: Writing `while lo <= hi`. When the pointers meet, the code adds `nums[lo]` to itself, so a target of 8 with a single 4 in the array reports a pair that does not exist.

check.question: Sorted nums = [1, 4, 5, 7, 10] and target 12. The first sum is 1 + 10 = 11. What happens next?
choices: hi moves left, because 11 is too small
lo moves right, because 11 is too small
Both pointers move inward
The scan stops: no pair can work
check.explanation: 11 is below the target, and 1's largest possible partner (10) was not enough, so 1 is eliminated and lo moves right. Moving hi left would make the sum even smaller.

sections.title: Palindromes: skip what does not count
sections.key: Compare characters from both ends and skip what does not count with inner loops that also check `lo < hi`: a palindrome check in O(1) space.
sections.body:
"A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" is a palindrome if you ignore case, spaces and punctuation. A cleaned, reversed copy works but costs O(n) space. Two pointers need O(1).

[[visual]]

The inner skip loops need their own `lo < hi` guard: on `".,!"` an unguarded `lo` walks off the end.

Digits are compared, not skipped: `"0P"` is not a palindrome. In Python, `ch.isalnum()` tests letters and digits (Unicode-aware) and `ch.lower()` normalizes case. JavaScript has no `isalnum`; `/[a-z0-9]/i` works for ASCII.

The "one deletion allowed" variant uses the same loop: at the first mismatch, check whether skipping the left or the right character leaves a palindrome.

visual.title: Checking a palindrome with two pointers

steps.label: Move lo right past anything that is not a letter or digit
Move hi left the same way
Do s[lo] and s[hi] differ, ignoring case?

sections.pitfall: Forgetting the `lo < hi` guard on the inner skip loops. On an input with no letters or digits, `lo` runs past the end: Python raises an error and JavaScript compares `undefined`.

check.question: Why does each inner skip loop also check lo < hi?
choices: To make the comparison case-insensitive
Because isalnum is slow and should be called less often
So that digits are skipped along with punctuation
So a string with no letters or digits cannot push a pointer past the other or off the end
check.explanation: Without the guard, ".,!" sends lo past every character and off the end of the string. The guard stops each skip as soon as the pointers meet. Case handling comes from lower(), and digits must not be skipped.

sections.title: Same direction: read and write pointers
sections.key: A read pointer visits every item and a write pointer marks where the next kept item goes, so `nums[:write]` is the finished part.
sections.body:
Remove duplicates from sorted `[0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3]` in place, and return k, the count of unique values now in `nums[:k]`.

- `read` visits every element.
- `write` marks the next slot. Invariant: `nums[:write]` holds the unique values seen so far, in order.

In sorted data duplicates are neighbors, so a value is new when it differs from `nums[write - 1]`, the last one written. Return 0 for an empty array; otherwise start write and read at 1 (the first value is always kept).

[[visual]]

O(n) time, O(1) space. The same skeleton removes a value, moves zeros, or keeps at most two of each (compare with `nums[write - 2]`).

On linked lists this becomes **fast and slow pointers**: fast moves two steps per slow step, finding the middle or a cycle.

visual.title: Deduplicating in place
visual.caption: Return write = 4. The first four slots hold `[0, 1, 2, 3]`; the rest is leftover data.

sections.code:
def remove_element(nums, val):          # remove every val in place
    write = 0
    for read in range(len(nums)):
        if nums[read] != val:
            nums[write] = nums[read]
            write += 1
    return write

def keep_at_most_two(nums):             # nums sorted
    write = 0
    for x in nums:
        if write < 2 or x != nums[write - 2]:
            nums[write] = x
            write += 1
    return write

b = [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]
k = keep_at_most_two(b)
print(k, b[:k])      # 6 [1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3]
sections.pitfall: Comparing with the wrong neighbor. Plain dedupe compares with `nums[write - 1]`, the last kept value. The at-most-two variant must compare with `nums[write - 2]`, not with the previous item read.

check.question: In the remove-duplicates loop on a sorted array, what does nums[:write] hold after each step?
choices: Every value seen so far, including repeats
The distinct values seen so far, in sorted order
The values that have not been read yet
The duplicates that will be removed
check.explanation: That is the invariant: a value is copied to nums[write] only when it differs from nums[write - 1], so the kept prefix holds each distinct value once, in order. Repeats are skipped and unread values sit after read, not before write.

sections.title: Sort first, then sweep: 3sum
sections.key: Sort, fix each first value, and run a pair-sum sweep on the rest; skip repeated first values and repeated `lo` values after a match. Total O(n^2).
sections.body:
Find all unique zero-sum triples in `[-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]`. Checking every triple is O(n^3); instead fix the first number, and the other two form a pair-sum problem.

- **Sort** to `[-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]`: O(n log n), less than the O(n^2) to come.
- **For each i**, find pairs in `nums[i + 1:]` that sum to `-nums[i]` with converging pointers.
- **Skip repeated first values:** if `nums[i] == nums[i - 1]`, skip i; the equal value before it found those triples.
- **After a match**, move both pointers, then keep moving `lo` while it equals the value just used.

[[visual]]

O(n^2) time: n choices of i, each an O(n) sweep, and O(1) extra space besides the output. Stop once `nums[i] > 0`.

visual.title: Trace on [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]
rows: Largest pair 1 + 2 = 3 is too small: none
1 + 2 = 3 is too big; the pointers meet
visual.caption: Result: `[[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]`.

sections.pitfall: Skipping duplicates by looking ahead (`nums[i] == nums[i + 1]`) instead of back. That skips the first copy of a value, so a triple using two copies, such as [-1, -1, 2], is never found.

check.question: Why can 3sum afford to sort the input first?
choices: Sorting removes the duplicates automatically
Sorting makes the whole algorithm O(n)
The problem guarantees the input is already sorted
Sorting is O(n log n), which is smaller than the O(n^2) search that follows
check.explanation: The total is O(n log n) + O(n^2) = O(n^2), so sorting is free in Big-O terms, and it is what makes the pair-sum sweep possible. Sorting keeps duplicates (it just puts them next to each other), which is why the skipping logic is needed.

sections.title: Container with most water: move the shorter side
sections.key: Start with the widest container and always move the shorter line: every narrower container that keeps it is capped at its height, so it cannot win.
sections.body:
Two lines from `[1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]` and the x-axis form a container holding `min(height[lo], height[hi]) * (hi - lo)`. Find the maximum. All pairs is O(n^2).

[[visual]]

Start at lo = 0 and hi = n - 1. Suppose `height[lo]` is shorter. Every container left to check is narrower, and any that keeps lo is still capped at `height[lo]`. So lo cannot beat the area just measured: discard it. Moving the taller line can never help.

[[visual 2]]

With equal heights, move either: a better container would need both lines taller, so it uses neither. This **greedy elimination** gives O(n) time and O(1) space.

visual.title: Line heights by index
visual.caption: Best pair: index 1 (height 8) and index 8 (height 7). Level 7, width 7, area 49.

visual.title: The first four steps
visual.caption: Every container after these is narrower and no taller, so the answer stays 49.

sections.pitfall: Moving the taller pointer, or both. In [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7], moving the taller side first discards the 7 at the right end before it pairs with the 8 at index 1, so 49 is never measured.

check.question: The pointers hold heights 4 (left) and 9 (right). Which pointer moves, and why?
choices: The left one: every remaining container using the 4 is narrower and still capped at 4
The right one: the 9 is too tall to hold water efficiently
Both, to shrink the range faster
Neither: from here you must try every remaining pair
check.explanation: The shorter line limits the level. Any later container with the 4 has a smaller width and a level of at most 4, so it cannot beat the current one; discard the 4. Moving the 9 can only shrink the width while the 4 still caps the level.

sections.title: Practice: choose the shape, avoid classic bugs
sections.key: Before coding, pick the shape, state the move rule and why it is safe, and choose the stop condition, usually `lo < hi`.
sections.body:
Decide three things before you write code:

- **Which shape?** Opposite ends for pairs and palindromes, same direction for in-place compaction, one pointer per sequence for merging.
- **What is the move rule, and why is it safe?** One sentence: "the sum is too big, so the right value cannot pair with anything left; move it."
- **When does it stop?** Usually `lo < hi` for converging pointers, the end of the array for same-direction scans.

[[visual]]

Converging and same-direction scans are O(n) time and O(1) space, because each pointer moves one way only. Sort-then-sweep adds O(n log n) for the sort.

Classic bugs and their fixes:

[[visual 2]]

visual.title: Problems and their move rules
rows: Sum too small: move lo; too big: move hi
Sort, fix i, pair sum on the rest, skip duplicates
Take the smaller head, advance it
Compare the ends' absolute values; fill the result from the back

visual.title: Bug to fix
rows: Move both pointers after recording it
Skip duplicates by comparing with the previous value
After a match, skip repeated `lo` values
Sort first, or use a hash map
A pointer runs off the end

activity.title: Container with most water
activity.prompt: Start with the widest container and always move the shorter line. Before you submit, trace [1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7] by hand and confirm you reach 49.

check.question: A function that collects every pair with a target sum in a sorted array loops forever on some inputs. Which bug is the likely cause?
choices: It uses lo < hi as the loop condition
It starts hi at len(nums) - 1
When it finds a match it records it but moves neither pointer
It compares the sum with the target using ==
check.explanation: If neither pointer moves after a match, the next iteration sees the same pair and records it again, forever. After a match, move both pointers inward (and skip duplicates if the problem wants unique pairs). The other choices are correct code.

keyTerms.definition: A technique that moves two indexes through one or two sequences so each step rules out possibilities, often replacing nested loops.
Pointers that start at both ends and move toward each other, as in pair sum on sorted data and palindrome checks.
Same-direction pointers where read scans everything and write marks where the next kept item goes.
Same-direction pointers moving at different speeds, used on linked lists to find the middle or detect a cycle.
A fact that stays true at every step of a loop, such as nums[:write] holding the kept items.
The proof that a pointer move is safe because the discarded element cannot be part of any remaining answer.
Sorting first so a two-pointer scan can follow, as in 3sum; the sort adds O(n log n).
Advancing past repeated values so each unique answer is reported once, by comparing with the previous value.

summary: Each pointer move rules something out for good, replacing nested loops.
Sorted pair sum: too small, move lo up; too big, move hi down; stop when they meet.
Read and write pointers compact in place; `nums[:write]` is finished.
3sum: sort, then a pair-sum sweep per first value, skipping duplicates: O(n^2).
Container with most water: always move the shorter line.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Using a sorted list of gift prices and a gift card balance, explain to a friend why moving the left or right pointer never skips a valid pair. Then explain why container with most water always moves the shorter line.

questions.question: Which situation most strongly suggests converging two pointers?
choices: The array is sorted and you need a pair with a target sum
You need the k most frequent values in an unsorted array
You must count how often each word appears
You need the shortest path in a maze
questions.explanation: Sorted data plus a pair condition is the signature of converging pointers: each comparison tells you which end to discard. Frequencies call for a hash map, and shortest paths for BFS.

questions.question: Match each problem with the two-pointer shape that solves it.

pairs.left: Check whether a string is a palindrome
Remove all zeros from an array in place
Find the middle node of a linked list

questions.explanation: Palindromes compare both ends. In-place filtering keeps a write position behind a read position. Merging advances whichever input has the smaller head. Fast and slow pointers reach the middle because fast covers twice the distance.

questions.question: Two sum on an unsorted array must return the original indexes. Why is sort-then-two-pointers awkward here?
choices: Two pointers cannot handle negative numbers
Sorting an array of integers takes O(n^2)
Sorting scrambles positions, so you would have to carry the original indexes along; a hash map solves it directly in O(n)
Two pointers only work on strings
questions.explanation: You could sort (value, index) pairs and then sweep, but that is O(n log n) and fiddly, while a hash map of value to index answers in one O(n) pass. Two pointers handle negatives fine, and sorting is O(n log n).
questions.concept: when not to use two pointers

questions.question: What property of a sorted array makes converging pointers work for pair sums?
questions.answer: Moving lo right can only keep or increase the sum, and moving hi left can only keep or decrease it. That predictable direction lets each comparison rule out one element for good.
questions.explanation: Without sorted order, moving a pointer could make the sum go either way, and you would have no basis for discarding an element.

questions.question: Converging pointers run on sorted nums = [1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 15] with target 15. What is the first sum computed?
questions.explanation: lo starts at index 0 (1) and hi at the last index (15), so the first sum is 1 + 15 = 16. It is too big, so hi moves left next.

questions.question: For sorted nums = [1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 15] and target 15, which pair of values does the converging scan find?
choices: 1 and 15
2 and 11
7 and 7
4 and 11
questions.explanation: 1 + 15 = 16, too big: hi moves to 11. 1 + 11 = 12, too small: lo moves to 2. 2 + 11 = 13: lo moves to 4. 4 + 11 = 15: found. There is only one 7, and an element cannot pair with itself.

questions.question: has_pair([1, 4, 6], 8) returns True, but no two items sum to 8. What is the bug?
choices: The loop must be while lo < hi; when lo == hi it adds 4 to itself
lo should start at 1
The two comparisons are reversed
It should return False as soon as total > target
questions.explanation: 1 + 6 = 7 moves lo to 1; 4 + 6 = 10 moves hi to 1. Now lo == hi and the loop still runs, computing 4 + 4 = 8. Stopping when the pointers meet prevents an element from pairing with itself.

questions.question: Fill the blank so the function counts pairs i < j with nums[i] + nums[j] < target in a sorted array.
choices: hi - lo
hi - lo + 1
lo - hi
questions.explanation: If nums[lo] + nums[hi] is below the target, nums[lo] pairs with every index from lo + 1 to hi, which is hi - lo pairs, because those values are no bigger than nums[hi]. Adding 1 misses most of them; hi - lo + 1 counts lo pairing with itself.

questions.question: count_pairs_below([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 7) counts pairs i < j whose sum is less than 7. What does it return?
questions.explanation: The pairs are 1+2, 1+3, 1+4, 1+5, 2+3 and 2+4. 3 + 4 = 7 is not below 7. In the scan, lo = 1 adds 4 at once (hi at index 4), then lo = 2 adds 2 once hi has moved to index 3.

questions.question: Why is it safe to move hi left when nums[lo] + nums[hi] > target?
choices: Every remaining partner for nums[hi] is at least nums[lo], so every pair using nums[hi] is also too big
nums[hi] is the largest value, and the largest value is never part of an answer
Moving lo would make the sum smaller
The answer is always in the left half of the array
questions.explanation: The remaining candidates sit between lo and hi and are all at least nums[lo], so pairing them with nums[hi] gives sums at least as large as the current, too-big sum. The largest value can be in an answer in general; it just cannot be in this one.

questions.question: Fill the blank in the skip loop of the palindrome check.
choices: hi -= 1
lo += 1
lo -= 1
break
questions.explanation: The left pointer skips characters that do not count by moving right. hi -= 1 would move the wrong pointer, and break would compare a punctuation mark.

questions.question: With the rule "lowercase everything and ignore anything that is not a letter or digit", is "0P" a palindrome?
choices: No, because "0" and "p" differ
Yes, because digits are ignored
Yes, because it has only two characters
It raises an error on the digit
questions.explanation: Digits are kept and compared, so the check compares "0" with "p" and fails. Solutions that keep only letters wrongly treat "0P" as "p", a classic bug.

questions.question: is_palindrome(".,") raises IndexError. Why?
choices: lower() fails on punctuation
hi should start at len(s)
The outer loop should be while lo <= hi
The inner loops lack a lo < hi guard, so lo runs off the end of a string with no letters or digits
questions.explanation: Both characters are punctuation, so the first inner loop moves lo to 1, then to 2, and s[2] does not exist. Guarding each skip loop with lo < hi stops it when the pointers meet.

questions.question: Which strings are palindromes under the rule "lowercase everything and ignore anything that is not a letter or digit"? Select all that apply.
choices: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"
"race a car"
"No 'x' in Nixon"
"ab_a"
questions.explanation: Cleaned, they become amanaplanacanalpanama, noxinnixon, the empty string and aba, which all read the same backward. race a car becomes raceacar, and 0P becomes 0p.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: 2 is written to index 1 and 3 to index 2, so k is 3. Indexes 3 and 4 are never written and keep their old values, 3 and 3. The list is not shortened; only the first k slots are guaranteed.

questions.question: nums is sorted. Fill the blank so each value is kept at most twice, in place.
choices: nums[write - 1]
nums[write]
nums[write - 2]
nums[-2]
questions.explanation: If x equals the value two slots back in the kept part, the kept part already has two copies of x. Comparing with nums[write - 1] would keep only one copy, which is plain dedupe.

questions.question: Removing duplicates in place from the sorted array [2, 2, 2, 5, 5, 9], what length k is returned?
questions.explanation: The distinct values are 2, 5 and 9, so k = 3 and the first three slots become [2, 5, 9].

questions.question: Which two-pointer shape finds the middle node of a linked list in one pass?
choices: Converging pointers from the head and the tail
Read and write pointers that copy values
Fast and slow pointers, where fast moves two steps for each step of slow
Binary search on the node values
questions.explanation: When fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the distance. A singly linked list cannot be walked backward from the tail, so converging pointers do not apply.

questions.question: Put the steps of in-place deduplication of a sorted array in order.
items: If the array is empty, return 0
Set write = 1, since the first value is always kept
For each read index from 1, compare nums[read] with nums[write - 1]
If they differ, copy nums[read] to nums[write] and increment write
questions.explanation: The empty check avoids writing past an empty array. Starting write at 1 keeps the first value. Comparing with the last kept value works because sorted duplicates are adjacent, and write ends as the number of unique values.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of the sort-then-sweep 3sum solution?
choices: O(n log n)
O(n)
questions.explanation: Sorting is O(n log n). Then for each of n first values, a converging sweep takes O(n), giving O(n^2), which dominates.

questions.question: This version returns [[-1, 0, 1]] for [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4] and misses [-1, -1, 2]. Why?
choices: range(len(nums) - 2) stops one index too early
Looking ahead skips the first -1, and the second -1 cannot use the first as a partner, so the triple with two -1s is lost
The inner duplicate skip should move hi instead of lo
Sorting separates the two -1s
questions.explanation: Sorted, the array is [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]. At i = 1 the look-ahead check sees another -1 and skips; at i = 2 the search only covers indexes 3 to 5, so the earlier -1 is out of reach. Comparing with nums[i - 1] (and requiring i > 0) keeps the first copy instead.

questions.question: After 3sum records a triple, why must it skip repeated values of nums[lo]?
choices: Otherwise lo could pass hi
Because the array is no longer sorted after a match
Otherwise the next lo with the same value can pair with an equal hi value and report the same triple again
To keep the algorithm at O(n log n)
questions.explanation: In [-2, 0, 0, 2, 2], fixing -2 finds [-2, 0, 2]; if lo only steps once it lands on another 0 while hi lands on another 2, and the same triple is recorded twice. The array stays sorted throughout, and the loop condition already stops lo passing hi.

questions.question: Which statements about the sort-then-sweep 3sum solution are true? Select all that apply.
choices: Sorting first costs O(n log n), which does not change the O(n^2) total
Once nums[i] > 0 after sorting, the outer loop can stop
It needs a hash map to avoid duplicate triples
For each i, the inner search is a pair-sum problem on nums[i + 1:]
It runs in O(n log n) overall
questions.explanation: Sorting is dominated by the O(n^2) sweeps. With a positive first value, all later values are positive too, so no triple can sum to zero. Duplicates are handled by skipping equal neighbors, no hash map needed, and the total is O(n^2), not O(n log n).

questions.question: How many unique triples summing to zero does [-2, 0, 1, 1, 2] contain?
questions.explanation: [-2, 0, 2] and [-2, 1, 1]. The two 1s are different elements, so [-2, 1, 1] is allowed, but it is counted once.

questions.question: Lines of height 3 at index 2 and height 8 at index 7 form a container. How much water does it hold?
questions.explanation: The shorter line caps the level at 3 and the width is 7 - 2 = 5, so the area is 3 x 5 = 15.

questions.question: In container with most water, the left pointer holds height 6 and the right pointer holds height 2. Which pointer moves?
choices: The left pointer, because it is taller
Both pointers
Whichever is farther from the middle
The right pointer, because the shorter line cannot be part of a better container
questions.explanation: Every remaining container is narrower, and any that keeps the height-2 line is still capped at 2, so none can beat the current one. Discard the 2 by moving the right pointer.

questions.question: max_area([1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]) returns 8 instead of 49. What is wrong?
choices: It moves the taller pointer; it should move lo when height[lo] < height[hi] and hi otherwise
The area should use max instead of min
The width should be hi - lo + 1
best should start at height[0]
questions.explanation: The comparison is flipped, so the code discards the taller line and keeps the short 1 at index 0 until the end, measuring only containers capped at height 1. Moving the shorter line keeps the tall lines in play and finds 8 and 7 at indexes 1 and 8.

questions.question: Explain why moving the shorter line in container with most water never skips the best answer.
questions.answer: Every container still to be checked is narrower than the current one. Any of them that uses the shorter line is capped at that line's height, so its area is smaller than the one just measured. The shorter line cannot be in a better container, so discarding it is safe.
questions.explanation: This elimination argument is the reason the greedy O(n) scan is correct, and interviewers usually ask for it.

questions.question: Given a sorted array that may contain negatives, return the squares of each number in sorted order in O(n). Which approach fits?
choices: Square everything, then sort; it is O(n) because the input was sorted
Converging pointers from both ends, filling the result from the largest square down
A hash map from each value to its square
Binary search for the position of each square
questions.explanation: The largest square is always at one of the two ends (the most negative or the most positive value), so compare the ends, place the bigger square at the back of the result, and move that pointer. Sorting the squares is O(n log n) no matter how the input was ordered.

questions.question: all_pairs([1, 2, 3, 4], 5) never returns. Why?
choices: The loop condition should be lo <= hi
pairs.append needs a list, not a tuple
After a match neither pointer moves, so the loop repeats the same comparison forever
The elif branches are reversed
questions.explanation: 1 + 4 = 5 matches on the first step and nothing changes lo or hi, so the same pair is appended forever. After recording a match, move both pointers inward.
